newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Two Koreas squabble over top Pyongyang defector.
newsitem.headline: Two Koreas squabble over top Pyongyang defector.

text.p: China was torn between loyalty to a socialist comrade and its new capitalist friend on Thursday as the two Koreas squabbled over the fate of a Pyongyang defector protected by Chinese troops in Seoul's mission in Beijing.

By late evening there was no sign of an end to the diplomatic impasse over Hwang Jang-yop, 73, a pillar of North Korea's Stalinist establishment, as Seoul and Pyongyang used pressure tactics on China to resolve the crisis.
Earlier on Thursday, South Korea released a letter from Hwang describing the agony of his flight from a starving nation he said had gone mad.
China deployed troops around the building, partly to stop North Koreans lurking in cars outside from bursting in.
And in an apparent sign of impatience with Seoul's loud-hailer diplomacy, Chinese officials avoided meeting an envoy sent by Seoul's foreign minister.
Seoul ordered heightened vigilance by its military and Pyongyang warned of unspecified countermeasures against South Korea, accusing Seoul authorities of kidnapping Hwang.
"I tormented and tormented over this," Hwang said in the four-page signed note written in the diplomatic compound, where he arrived with an aide by taxi on Wednesday.
"Starting with my family, people will judge that I'm mad. But the question is: am I the only mad person?"
Hwang attacked those in the North who continued to treat South Korea as the enemy and talked of turning it into a "sea of fire" while proposing national unification.

"How could you regard this as the behaviour of sane people?," asked Hwang, one of the architects of Pyongyang's "Juche" philosophy of fanatic self-reliance and now the most senior official ever to seek refuge in the South.
"Also, how could you call people sane who loudly talk about building an ideal society for workers and farmers while workers and farmers are starving?"

South Korean radio reported from Beijing on Thursday that according to a senior Chinese official, North Korea was sending a high-ranking delegation to the Chinese capital on Friday to discuss the Hwang case.
But diplomats said it was likely that South Korea, which has been pouring investment into China in recent years, would prevail in its attempts to have Hwang brought to Seoul.
South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha arrived in Singapore for a Friday morning meeting with his Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen to lobby for Hwang's safe passage.
The two Koreas traded accusations of cloak-and-dagger treachery among the tree-shaded avenues of Beijing's sedate diplomatic district.
Seoul rejected as "preposterous" Pyongyang's assertion that Hwang was a kidnap victim and complained that North Koreans had tried to barge in to the compound during the night.

Adding weight to suspicions that South Korea may have had advance notice of Hwang's flight, Seoul intelligence authorities released a family portrait showing the official at home with his well-dressed wife, son and grandchildren.

In the foreground of the photo, a round dining table is laden with tropical fruits, an unimaginable luxury for most North Koreans who have been driven by food shortages into foraging for edible grass and roots.
In a separate letter purportedly written by Hwang before his defection and splashed in the Chosun Ilbo newspaper, Hwang denounced a socialist system that had led to food shortages.
"How can a society of people, workers, farmers and intelligentsia dying of hunger be called socialist?" he asked.

"The great general's self-admiration has gone so far that he now really believes he is a genius, requiring the people to respect and obey him only," he said in an attack on North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.

In Geneva on Thursday U.N. and aid officials said North Korea would need foreign supplies by April if starvation was to be averted. On Wednesday the Rome-based U.N. World Food Programme said North Koreans were receiving a quarter of their minimum daily food needs.
South and North Korea were split at the end of World War Two and fought a war from 1950 to 1953, with China battling on the North's side in the conflict.
Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said Hwang was apparently a marked man when he was in Tokyo this month for a conference on "Juche".
Hashimoto told reporters Hwang's bodyguards may have been tipped off to his plans and shadowed him more closely towards the end of his visit.

Japan also expressed concern the row could derail Korean peace efforts that appeared to be back on track after Pyongyang apologised for an incursion into Southern waters by one of its submarines in September.
"We had not anticipated such a defection at all," Hashimoto's spokesman, Seiroku Kajiyama, told reporters.
"We once had hopes for some progress in dialogue between South and North Korea after Pyongyang's apology for the submarine incident, and I hope such prospects will not be diminished due to this."
Hwang is ranked 24th in North Korea's power structure by Seoul officials and is one of 11 secretaries on the powerful secretariat of the ruling Workers' Party.
